findings.quote: Methadone is a μ opioid receptor agonist and effects are enantioselective. R‐methadone exerts the majority of the opioid effects of the racemate because it has 30‐ to 50‐fold higher binding affinity and analgesic potency than S‐methadone.
findings.text: Methadone acts as a mu opioid receptor agonist, with R-methadone providing most of the opioid effects due to having 30- to 50-fold higher binding affinity and analgesic potency than S-methadone.

findings.quote: Methadone also interacts with norepinephrine and serotonin reuptake transporters at concentrations which more closely resemble those achieved clinically.
findings.text: Methadone interacts with norepinephrine and serotonin reuptake transporters at concentrations similar to those achieved in clinical settings.

findings.quote: methadone blocks N‐methyl‐D‐aspartate (NMDA) receptors in laboratory studies. However, clinical methadone concentrations (often < 1 μM) are lower than the IC50 or Ki of methadone for the NMDA receptor (3–10 μM).
findings.text: In laboratory studies, methadone blocks NMDA receptors, but clinical concentrations are lower than the levels required for this effect.

limits.quote: R‐methadone appears more potent than S‐methadone at these non‐opioid receptors. Whether this influences methadone‐induced analgesia is unknown.
limits.text: It is unknown if the potency of R-methadone at non-opioid receptors influences the pain relief caused by methadone.
